The study identifies inosine as a purine metabolite associated with improved overall survival in human renal cell carcinoma (RCC) patients treated with nivolumab (anti-PD1). Specifically, higher baseline plasma levels of inosine were correlated with longer median overall survival (33 months vs. 22 months for low levels) in the CheckMate 025 trial cohort (n=743 RCC patients, 394 treated with nivolumab). The study also notes that gut microbiota dysbiosis induced by ICB treatment affects plasma purine metabolite levels, and references prior work linking specific bacterial genera (Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium) to inosine production.

The study reports clinical cohort data linking fecal Short-Chain Fatty Acid (SCFA) concentrations to Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor (ICI) outcomes. Specifically, in a cohort of 52 solid tumor patients receiving anti-PD-1 therapy (nivolumab or pembrolizumab), higher fecal concentrations of acetate, propionate, butyrate, and valerate were significantly associated with longer progression-free survival [29]. Additionally, in a smaller cohort of 11 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients receiving second-line nivolumab, gut microbial metabolites including propionate and butyrate were significantly associated with long-term beneficial effects [34]. The study also notes that serum TMAO concentrations were positively correlated with progression-free survival and ICI response in clinical data [37], and a combination of plasma metabolites (hippuric acid, butyrylcarnitine, cysteine, glutathione disulfide) showed high accuracy for predicting PD-1 blockade response in NSCLC patients [52].

The study discusses Inosine as a purine metabolite produced by Bifidobacterium pseudolongum and Mucorophilus, noting it can up-regulate IL12Rβ2 and IFNγ transcription to promote Th1 cell differentiation in the TME.

The study mentions that 'in vitro physiological concentrations of inosine enhance Th1 differentiation and effector function', but does not provide specific quantitative values (e.g., μM) for these concentrations or their levels in human serum/TME.
The study describes Butyric acid (a short-chain fatty acid) as increasing ID2 expression in CD8+ T cells and inhibiting HDAC class I enzymes to reprogram them, enhancing anti-tumor activity.

The study notes that butyric and valeric acids are produced from undigested carbohydrates digested by colonic anaerobes, but does not report measured physiological concentrations in human cohorts linked to ICI outcomes.
